1dgdcg5:305: The agent runtime only holds three IDs (Payment Manager ARN, Payment Instrument ID, Payment Session ID) and cannot see the private key, Payment Connector, or Payment Credential Provider. 1h511bw:244: maxSpendAmount is enforced at the server-side Payment Session validation layer, not implemented as a soft constraint in agent code via system prompt. This is a fundamental difference — prompt injection can bypass any spending limit written in the prompt, but it cannot forge or tamper with the server-side session validation result. From a defense-in-depth perspective, this layer is the cornerstone of the agent payment security architecture: if the budget constraint exists at the code layer, an attacker needs only to control the agent's reasoning process to bypass it; if it is server-side, the attack surface narrows to parameter injection when calling the API, and the harm boundary is quantifiable.

1n351tm:330: The three-layer object design of Payment Manager (business-line granularity), Payment Instrument (chain/currency), and Payment Session (scenario granularity) makes budget control highly flexible — under the same business line you can attach Instruments for multiple chains, and under each Instrument you can open different Sessions per task. The three session granularities — "single purchase 0.01 USDC," "current task cap 1 USDC," "monthly cumulative 100 USDC" — correspond to different business risk levels and can be managed independently on the control plane without modifying agent code. Because Payment Instrument is a wallet reference rather than the wallet itself, switching wallet backends at runtime (from Coinbase CDP to Stripe Privy) requires no agent code changes.

x5soql:17: 1. Responsibility boundary between payment protocol and custodial service
xgrvvv:208: The x402 protocol only solves "how the two parties negotiate," while AgentCore Payments solves "how an agent securely pays money within an organization." These two layers are architecturally orthogonal in responsibility — the protocol layer defines payment syntax, and the hosted service layer defines payment semantics. Without this intermediate layer, even if an agent can negotiate payment terms, it has no trusted execution environment; without the protocol layer, the hosted service can only function as a local wallet and cannot interconnect with arbitrary sellers. When designing an agent payment system, you must first define this boundary in the architecture, rather than trying to use one layer to cover the other.
